sermon.title: Many Adversaries Part 1
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer teaches from 1 Corinthians 16 on the first day of the week and why Saturday or Sunday is a “silly” argument, then on Paul’s “great door” with “many adversaries.” He lists nine kinds of opposition believers face, then answers critics who say the Bible is wrong about slavery, shellfish and other things.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, capitalization and paragraphing were added by hand, and obvious caption errors were corrected; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. Editor note: the recording plays or reads several quotes from public speakers (about 11:12–17:50); the captions do not mark where each begins and ends, and the pastor names only one speaker. For the slavery claim he names the speaker, and in the second part refers to “Mr. Obama” and a talk-show host; those names appear in the transcript only, not in the short answers. In the quote about public policy, the names after “James” and “Al” were garbled in the captions and are marked [unclear] rather than guessed. The caption “$2.5 million” may have been “billion” (he gives both figures in the sentence); it is left as captioned. He says “in Psalms it says your enemies will be those of your own household”; the words are in Micah 7:6 (and Matthew 10:36), shown here. “[Unclear]” marks nine spots where the captions were not clear, including the start of Acts 16:16 (the caption reads “1616”) and the two names in the public-policy quote.

chunks.section_question: Why did the early church meet on the first day of the week?
chunks.short_answer: He cites Luke 24:1, Acts 20:7 and Revelation 1:10 to show the disciples met on the first day of the week because Jesus rose from the grave on that day. He says history shows Roman reports that Christians “meet on the first day of the week,” though Acts also shows them in the synagogue on Saturday.
chunks.text:
We are in chapter 16 of 1 Corinthians, in verses 1-4. He talks about collecting for the saints that are in Jerusalem on the first day of the week: take up the collection, so when I come there’s no collections to be taken up. And, uh, there’s a big argument in America and throughout the world on what day we should serve Jesus, what day we should come to church, Saturday or Sunday. In Luke 24:1 we find that on the first day of the week Jesus rose from the grave, on Easter Sunday, the first day of the week. So see, they met on Sunday, the first day of the week, because Jesus rose from the grave. We find in Acts 20:7 that on the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached to them until one guy fell out of the window.

See, they say I’m a long-winded preacher here, but let me tell you, Paul has got me beat by a long shot. But anyway, they met together on the first day of the week. When you study history, you will find that Roman rulers, lower ranks in authority, would have to report to higher ranks, and they would say, “These Christians meet on the first day of the week, and they take communion, and they make a vow that they will not commit adultery and, and, uh, steal and, and do these bad things, on the first day of the week.” So there’s plenty of evidence that the early church met on the first day of the week. But also, if you read Acts, you’ll find them coming into the synagogue on Saturday also. They were there Saturday and Sunday if they could be. Revelations 1:10, John the apostle was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day. Now, what’s the Lord’s Day? The first day of the week, Sunday. So do we meet together on Sunday, or do we meet together on Saturday? And let me tell you, there’s a big argument out there. I debated out at the college with a bunch of college students about this thing. They, they just get young Christians wrapped up in silly things like Saturday or Sunday. It’s just a, a silly thing.

chunks.section_question: Does it matter whether we meet on Saturday or Sunday? (Colossians 2:16)
chunks.short_answer: He calls the Saturday-or-Sunday argument “a silly thing” and cites Colossians 2:16, “Let no man judge you in food or drink or in respect of a holiday or the new moon,” saying these are “shadow of things to come.” He cites Acts 1:3 and 1:14 to show Jesus was seen on any day, and says God “don’t care what day of the week it is.”
chunks.text:
As we see, Colossians 2:16 sums it up this way: “Let no man judge you in food or drink or in respect of a holiday or the new moon or the” what? “Sabbath days. Let no man judge you.” These are a what? “Shadow of things to come.” Say that with me: shadow of things to come. So you know the shadow isn’t the real thing, right? You know, your shadow isn’t the real thing. It brings you to the real thing. And so the Sabbath day was just an example of something God wanted to teach us.

All right, let’s, in Acts chapter 1:3, after Jesus rose from the grave, He was seen of them 40 days. Was He only seen of them on Sunday? Was He only seen of them on Saturday? No. He was seen of them anytime that they would accept seeing Him: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Acts 1:14, the 120 people in the upper room continued 10 days in prayer. The Bible says in one place. So did they leave on Monday? Did they leave on Tuesday? Would God turn His back on them if they met on Monday? No. Oh, come on, church. God’s so excited about you coming before Him, He don’t care what day of the week it is. And so it’s important that you understand that whether we meet on Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday, God accepts you coming together and seeking Him. Can I hear an amen? And we need to get rid of these silly little things that we argue and fight about and get on the real thing.

chunks.section_question: Why does Paul say a great door has opened but there are many adversaries? (1 Corinthians 16:5-9)
chunks.short_answer: He says Paul will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, a populated city where 12 people were filled with the Holy Ghost and bodies were healed through pieces of his garment, so that “All Asia has heard the word of God.” Paul says “a great and effective door has opened,” but there are many adversaries, or opponents.
chunks.text: Now he goes on to say in verses 5-8 that he’s going to stay in Ephesus till Pentecost, then he’s going to leave and pass through Corinth. And Ephesus, as you probably know by your history, is a populated city of 300,000 when Paul was there. And Paul went there, and 12 people were filled with the Holy Ghost in Ephesus to start his ministry there. And then parts of his clothing was sent out all through Asia, and bodies were healed and demons were cast out with just little pieces of his garment. And Paul said, “All Asia has heard the word of God,” and he’s writing to the Corinthians, and he says, “From Ephesus a great and effective door has opened for me here in Ephesus.” A powerful door. All these things are happening. The word of God is going out through all Asia, and talking about the Middle East, Asia Minor. But he says there are many what? Adversaries. There’s many opponents.

The second is those in the church who oppose with false teaching, such as saying there is no resurrection or that incest is okay.
chunks.text: Now let me give you a quick list of some opponents. You ready? Number one: we are the biggest opponent. Opponent means opposer. Opposer of the Scriptures, opposer of truth, opposer of God. He says, “in meekness instruct those who” what? “Oppose themselves.” We are our big, worst enemy. “We’re not good enough,” “we’re too good,” you know, “we’ve done the unpardonable sin,” you know, uh, we are our own worst enemy. “I’m so bad I can’t come to God now, God can’t change my life.” Number two, 1 Corinthians 15:12: “Some among you say there is no resurrection of the dead.” Then you got the problem with opposing in the church. Some among you say there’s no resurrection of the dead. Some among you say incest is okay. See, some among you are saying it’s okay to eat food sacrificed to idols and go into the idol temple and eat. Some of you have got these weird doctrines. But none of you. Right? Nobody in here. See, we oppose ourselves in the church, and we could go on and on. I taught, I taught on that; you can get the series.

chunks.section_question: Do governments, religious leaders and Satan oppose believers?
chunks.short_answer: He lists Jewish religious leaders commanding the disciples not to speak in Jesus’ name (Acts 4:18), a violent attempt to stone them (Acts 14:5), and the king who killed James with the sword (Acts 12:1). He says “government opposes us, church leaders oppose us,” and Satan hindered Paul (1 Thessalonians 2:18).
chunks.text: Number three, Acts 4:18: Jewish religious leaders commanded them to not speak or teach in the name of Jesus. Number four, a violent attempt was made by both the Gentile and the Jews, with their rulers, to abuse and stone the disciples, Acts 14:5. Number five, Acts 12:1, Herod the king, direct from Rome, his connection was straight to Rome, “stretched forth his hands to pain some of the church.” He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. See, government opposes us, church leaders oppose us, we oppose ourself, and our believing brothers oppose. There’s a lot of opposition. Number six, 1 Thessalonians 2:18: “We would have come unto you, but Satan hindered us.” Then we got Satan, our adversary, the Devil, as a roaring lion. He’s always trying to seduce us away from what’s right.

He also says false brethren fool Christians who don’t know their Bible, and that Scripture “is the high authority of God.”

chunks.section_question: What hardships did the apostles endure to preach the gospel?
chunks.short_answer: He says the apostles “went without food,” worked and went without sleep trying to preach the gospel. He says “it takes work to serve God,” but that Paul says all these adversaries are there alongside a great door of opportunity.
chunks.text: Hallelujah. And then you got to work, you got hunger. You think you got it tough? These apostles had it tough. They went without food, they worked, and they went without sleep, trying to preach the gospel. Now, they’re not like a lot of American pastors who play golf five days a week and then come in, give their bell-ringing message, and then go back and [unclear]. These guys worked hard. Are you there? And it takes work to serve God. And so he says all these adversaries are there, but there’s a great door of opportunity, great door.

chunks.section_question: Are people in high places teaching that the Bible should not guide public policy?
chunks.short_answer: He says homosexuals have been teaching this message since the ’70s to undermine the Bible’s influence, and that it has reached “people in high places.” He then reads a quote saying America is not just a Christian nation and asking which passages of Scripture should guide public policy, and says, “let’s read our Bibles.”

Okay. Now, the homosexuals have been teaching this message since the ‘70s, trying to rip the Bible apart and, and undermine it and destroy its influence in America, and it has influenced people in high places. chunks.section_question: Is there only one way to God?
chunks.short_answer: He plays a clip in which a speaker says there are many paths to what you call God, then responds, “There is one way and only one way, and that is true, Jesus.” He says the speaker is influential all over the world and “has accepted this doctrine,” and he plays another clip on whether Christians and Muslims worship the same God and whether the Bible is literally true.
chunks.text:
“One of the mistakes that human beings make is believing that there is only one way to live, and that we don’t accept that there are diverse ways of being in the world, that there are millions of ways to be a human being, and many ways— no, but many paths to what you call God. And her path might be something else, and when she gets there she might call it the light, but her loving and her kindness and her generosity brings her— if it brings her to the same point that it brings you, it doesn’t matter whether she called it God along the way or not. And I guess the danger that could be on that, I mean, it sounds great on the onset, but if you really look at both, besides, there couldn’t possibly be just one way. What? What about Jesus? What about Jesus?” And you say there isn’t only one way? There is one way and only one way, and that is true, Jesus. “There couldn’t possibly be—“

chunks.section_question: What does the Bible mean by servants, and did Paul approve of slavery?
chunks.short_answer: He says the Old Testament word for servant meant servanthood: you got into debt and worked it off, and “at the end of every seven years, all servants were free,” like indentured servants coming to America. He cites Matthew 19:19, says Paul’s words to submit to masters were “just telling them to keep a good attitude,” and says “the Bible never, from Genesis to Revelation, promotes slavery.”
chunks.text:
When the, the word servant or slave in the Old Testament really is a word that means servanthood. You got into debt and you couldn’t pay off your debt, so you had to become a servant of somebody that would pay your debt, and then you worked it off, and you couldn’t work any more than seven years. At the end of every seven years, all servants were free. See, people came from Europe to America on being indentured servants. The businessmen in America would pay their way, and then they worked off their way over, the price it cost to get over there, by serving that guy for so many years. See, it wasn’t slavery, it was a mutual agreement.

Are you there, church? Matthew 19:19: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” Now, how am I going to believe in slavery if I’m not willing to be a slave? You see, the Bible plainly says slavery was not accepted, and because they don’t understand the Bible, they twist these things around. Is that clear to you? The Bible never, from Genesis to Revelation, promotes slavery, never. When Paul wrote about slavery and told them to submit to their masters, he was just telling them to keep a good attitude, a right attitude, because there’s nothing you can do about it anyway. The government had passed a law for slaves, and just, he’s trying to tell them, you know, keep a good attitude in it. Ain’t that right? Not saying that slavery is okay. Now, how many raise your hand, said Mr. Savage is wrong? Yes. And people are believing this nonsense. They are believing this nonsense that these people are saying.

chunks.section_question: Is eating shellfish a sin? (Deuteronomy 14:21 and 1 Timothy 4:4)
chunks.short_answer: He cites Deuteronomy 14:21 and asks whether eating shellfish, catfish or shark would put you in hell, answering that the food laws were there “to remind them to live holy.” He cites 1 Timothy 4:4 that every creature of God is good and nothing is to be refused if it is received with thanksgiving.
chunks.text: Now let’s go to food, clothing, uh, farming, and these other things that he said the Bible is wrong on, and let’s take a close look at them. Are you ready? Deuteronomy 14:21: “You shall not eat anything that dies of itself. Give it to the stranger, the foreigner in the gates, or sell it to the alien, that he may eat it, for you are a holy people unto the Lord.” Now, why did God make these kind of laws? Was shellfish bad for anybody? Was eating shellfish going to put you into hell? Catfish was forbidden. If you eat catfish, you’re going to go to hell? Sharks were forbidden ‘cause they didn’t have scales. If you eat a shark, you’re going to go to hell? It wasn’t there for that. It was there to remind them to live holy. It says it right there, and the foreigners could eat it. Does God love the world? Does God love all nations? Is He going to allow one people to eat something that’s going to hurt them and another people, no? No. What’s He doing? He’s trying to teach the people and remind them to live holy, to live for God, to live right. That’s— continue. 1 Timothy 4:4: “Every creature”— how many creatures? Every creature, every animal— “of God is good, and nothing is to be refused for food if it is received with thanksgiving.” Now, is that plain? Yeah, you see—

faqs.question: What does 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 say about collecting for the saints?
faqs.answer: He says Paul talks about collecting for the saints in Jerusalem on the first day of the week, so that when he comes “there’s no collections to be taken up.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given orders to the churches of Galatia, so you must do also: On the first day of the week let each one of you lay something aside, storing up as he may prosper, that there be no collections when I come. And when I come, whomever you approve by your letters I will send to bear your gift to Jerusalem. But if it is fitting that I go also, they will go with me.

faqs.question: Did the early Christians meet only on Sunday?
faqs.answer: He says no: they also came into the synagogue on Saturday, and “they were there Saturday and Sunday if they could be.” He says the early church met on the first day of the week, and John was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day.

scriptures.text_nkjv: I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day, and I heard behind me a loud voice, as of a trumpet,

faqs.question: Would God turn His back on people who meet on a Monday?
faqs.answer: He says no: “God’s so excited about you coming before Him, He don’t care what day of the week it is.” He points to the 120 in the upper room who continued 10 days in prayer.

scriptures.text_nkjv: These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with His brothers.

faqs.question: How big was Ephesus, and what happened there?
faqs.answer: He says Ephesus was “a populated city of 300,000” when Paul was there. He says 12 people were filled with the Holy Ghost to start Paul’s ministry there, and pieces of his garment were sent out and bodies were healed and demons cast out.

scriptures.text_nkjv: Now I will come to you when I pass through Macedonia (for I am passing through Macedonia). And it may be that I will remain, or even spend the winter with you, that you may send me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now on the way; but I hope to stay a while with you, if the Lord permits. But I will tarry in Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

faqs.question: What does he say about thinking “I’m so bad I can’t come to God”?
faqs.answer: He says that is one way we oppose ourselves: “I’m so bad I can’t come to God now, God can’t change my life.” He says the opposite error is “we’re too good,” and that either way “we are our own worst enemy.”

faqs.question: Who does he say killed James, the brother of John?
faqs.answer: He says Herod the king, “direct from Rome,” stretched forth his hands to pain some of the church and killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.

scriptures.text_nkjv: Now about that time Herod the king stretched out his hand to harass some from the church. Then he killed James the brother of John with the sword.

faqs.question: What does he say Satan is always trying to do?
faqs.answer: He says Satan, our adversary, is “as a roaring lion,” and he’s “always trying to seduce us away from what’s right.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.

faqs.question: Does he say racial problems and family opposition are new?
faqs.answer: He says no: “Every generation thinks they’re new. They’ve been around forever.” He says our own nationality can reject us and tells of a war between two tribes in Ghana as an example of racial hatred.

faqs.question: How does he compare Bible servanthood to indentured servants?
faqs.answer: He says people came from Europe to America as indentured servants: businessmen paid their way and they worked off the price by serving that man for so many years. He says “it wasn’t slavery, it was a mutual agreement.”

faqs.question: What attitude does he say Paul told slaves to keep?
faqs.answer: He says when Paul told them to submit to their masters, he was telling them to “keep a good attitude, a right attitude, because there’s nothing you can do about it anyway.” He says Paul was not saying slavery is okay.

faqs.question: Why does he say some foods were forbidden in the law?
faqs.answer: He says the law was not there to send you to hell for eating shellfish or shark: “it was there to remind them to live holy.” He notes foreigners could eat it, and asks if God would allow one people to eat something that hurts them and not another.
